old: Each time, each can cooperate or cheat, and cheating pays unless both do it.
new: Each time, each can cooperate or cheat (from here on, defect), and cheating pays unless both do it.
why: The page says "cheat" here and "defect" everywhere after, with no sign that they are the same thing. The figures print "defects", so that word has to stay; this ties the two together once.

old: Now and then a move comes out wrong.
new: Now and then a move comes out wrong; I call that a slip.
why: The same thing is later called slips, noise, errors, mistakes and moves that went wrong. This gives it one name at first mention, and adds nothing else.

old: I let a hundred small machines breed and mutate to find out, and when a few moves in a hundred went wrong they kept arriving at the same machine of three states.
new: I let a hundred small machines, each one a way of playing, breed and mutate to find out, and when a few moves in a hundred slipped, the population kept ending up with the same machine.
why: A stranger does not know what a "machine" is here, and stops at "of three states". "Each one a way of playing" ties machine to the question just asked ("Which ways of playing survive?"). "Of three states" is cut from the opening only; the number is still given lower down.

old: It had been described in 2006, and analysed more thoroughly than I managed in 2012.
new: It had been described in 2006, and in 2012 it was analysed more thoroughly than I managed.
why: As printed it reads at first as "than I managed in 2012".

"The bed", "its kind" and "its own twin" are private words. This says that the bed is the live page, that a plant is a machine (as the picture's description already says), and that the twin is a copy of itself.

old: Set the slips to nothing and wait: cooperation arrives in brief spikes and is eaten each time.
new: You can open the bed and try it. Set the slips to nothing and wait: cooperation arrives in brief spikes and is lost again each time.
why: The paragraph gives instructions before saying there is anything to open; the only link is in the caption and the picture. "Eaten" is a figure of speech with no eater named.

old: Set them to between 1% and 3%, with long games, and after a while a kind that opens with two thorns tends to take the bed and hold it.
new: Set the slips to between 1% and 3%, with long games, and after a while a kind of machine whose plant begins with two thorns tends to take over the bed and hold it.
why: "A kind that opens with two thorns" asks the reader to hold three private words at once (kind, opens, thorns). Still "a kind", not "the kind", as you had it.

old: It can take tens of thousands of generations for anything to happen, and that is part of the result.
new: It can take tens of thousands of generations for anything to happen.
why: "That is part of the result" is a riddle as it stands: the page never says why. Cut it, or say why (see N05 in needs-author.json).

old: <figcaption>The machine at play, round by round, with no slips except the one outlined.</figcaption>
new: <figcaption>Four short games, one square to a round: C where a player cooperates, D where it defects. Nothing slips except the one move outlined. The fourth game belongs to the next section.</figcaption>
why: The caption did not say how to read the picture, and the fourth game shows a machine the text has not yet introduced. All of this is in the picture and its description already.

old: The machine defects until the other side has defected twice running.
new: The machine defects until the other side has defected twice in a row.
why: "Twice running" is not known to every reader of English.

old: Then it cooperates for as long as they do, and any defection sends it back to the start.
new: Then it cooperates for as long as they do, and a defection from them sends it back to the start.
why: "Any defection" left it open whose. The first game in the strip shows it is the other side's: the machine that slips in round 8 cooperates in round 9, and only the other one goes back. (Narrower than the old wording, not wider; the second reader should check it against the machine's table.)

old: Two of them open with two rounds of mutual defection and cooperate from then on.
new: So two of these machines spend their first two rounds defecting against each other, and cooperate from then on (the first game above).
why: Plainer than "mutual defection", and points at the game that shows it.

old: A slip costs about three rounds to repair.
new: When one of them slips, it takes about three rounds for the pair to get back to cooperating.
why: Says what is being repaired.

old: The opening is the point.
new: Those two opening defections are the point.
why: "The opening" has not been named as a thing yet.

old: In a world of plain reciprocators, players who simply always cooperate do just as well, drift in unnoticed, and then cheats feed on them.
new: In a world of plain reciprocators, who repay like with like, players who simply always cooperate do just as well. They drift in unnoticed, and then defectors feed on them.
why: This sentence carries the whole idea of the page and was the one I had to read twice. "Reciprocators" gets a four-word gloss (it is what the word means), the sentence is split, and "cheats" becomes "defectors" to keep one name.

old: A player who always cooperates never gets through this opening, so that door is shut.
new: Against this machine, a player who always cooperates never gets through the opening (the second game above), so that door is shut.
why: Says against whom, and points at the game that shows it.

old: And because slips keep happening, the machine's punishment is in constant use and does not wither.
new: And because slips keep happening, the machine's way of punishing a defection is in constant use and does not wither.
why: "The machine's punishment" arrives without having been mentioned; this says what is punished.

old: With the payoffs I used, one defection is not enough.
new: With the points I used (the payoffs), one defection is not enough.
why: "Payoffs" is a term of the trade; the page itself says "a point" lower down. The word is kept once in brackets because two of the figures print it.

old: Cheating a cooperator pays 5, mutual cooperation 3, mutual defection 1.
new: Defecting against a cooperator pays 5 points; when both cooperate each gets 3, and when both defect each gets 1.
why: Three numbers arrived without saying who gets them. "Each gets" is what the small print in the first picture says (1 a round if everyone defects, 3 if everyone cooperates).

old: A player who always defects collects 5 and 1 by turns from the one-defection machine, which averages 3, exactly what two cooperators earn.
new: A player who always defects collects 5 and 1 by turns from the one-defection machine (the fourth game above), which averages 3 a round, exactly what cooperators earn from each other.
why: Points at the game that shows it, and says the 3 is per round and per player.

old: With two defections in the opening the cheat is paid only every third round and falls behind.
new: With two defections in the opening, the player who always defects collects the 5 only every third round (the third game) and falls behind.
why: One name for this player (it was "a player who always defects" one sentence earlier and "the cheat" here). "Is paid only every third round" was loose: by the page's own points it collects 1 in the other rounds and the 5 in every third. The second reader should check this against the third game.

old: That condition on the payoffs was known too.
new: That it turns on the points in this way was known too.
why: "Condition on the payoffs" is a checker's phrase.

old: It is Fortress3, which Ashlock and Ashlock (2006) found in evolving populations of automata. Its table and mine match arrow for arrow.
new: It is Fortress3, which Ashlock and Ashlock (2006) found in evolving populations of machines of this sort (automata). Its rules and mine match exactly.
why: "Automata" is a third name for the machines; kept once in brackets for anyone searching. No table or arrows have been shown to the reader, so "arrow for arrow" means nothing here.

old: Why it holds.
new: Why it holds its ground.
why: "Holds" what? I first read it as "why it is true".

old: They went through every machine with up to three states, tested each as an equilibrium against all possible strategies when moves are noisy, and singled this one out.
new: They went through every machine with up to three states, tested each against all possible ways of playing when moves are noisy, and singled this one out.
why: "Equilibrium" is not explained and "strategies" is a second name for "ways of playing". This version only drops and renames; it says less than before, not more. A fuller plain version is N06 in needs-author.json. "Noisy" is left as it was on purpose: see N06.

old: That mistakes are what make such a strategy stable.
new: That mistakes are what make such a way of playing stable.
why: One name: "way of playing", as in the opening paragraph.

old: What my runs may add is small, and I have not searched for each piece: the same exhaustive test carried on to machines of four and five states, 3.76 million of them; and what happens as the population grows, which is the first thing I got wrong.
new: What my runs may add is small, and I have not searched for each piece. One piece is the same exhaustive test carried on to machines of four and five states, 3.76 million of them. The other is what happens as the population grows, which is the first thing I got wrong (below).
why: One sentence of 47 words with a colon and a semicolon, in which the list starts before the reader knows a list is coming. Same words, three sentences.

old: Even that may not be mine. Ashlock and Ashlock's paper is titled for changes "with different population sizes", and I have read only its abstract.
new: Even that may not be mine: the title of Ashlock and Ashlock's paper speaks of changes "with different population sizes", and I have read only its abstract, the summary at its head.
why: "Is titled for changes" is not English a stranger will parse. "Abstract" gets its meaning at first use.

old: <figcaption>Cooperation with and without slips, in evolving populations of three sizes.</figcaption>
new: <figcaption>The share of moves that are cooperative in evolving populations of three sizes, with no slips (blue) and with 2% of moves slipping (orange). Among a hundred machines there is more cooperation with slips; among a thousand there is more without them.</figcaption>
why: The caption named the subject and not the point. Everything here is in the picture, its description, or the first item of the list beneath it.

old: I wrote that a little noise doubles cooperation.
new: I wrote that a few slips double cooperation.
why: One name: slips. (This is your own claim about your own runs, so the renaming is safe; I have not renamed "noise" where it reports other people's papers.)

old: What slips change at every size is who does the cooperating: tit-for-tat and its kin without them, this machine with them.
new: What slips change at every size is who does the cooperating: without slips it is tit-for-tat and its kin, with slips it is this machine.
why: The old order makes the reader carry "them" back twice. Tit-for-tat is still unexplained: see N08 in needs-author.json.

old: I wrote that no strategy of any complexity could gain more than a thousandth of a point a round against the machine.
new: I wrote that no way of playing, however complicated, could gain more than a thousandth of a point a round against the machine.
why: One name: "way of playing". What the gain is measured from is still unsaid: see N09.

old: One who can tell gains about 0.19 a round when 5% of moves slip.
new: An opponent who can tell gains about 0.19 of a point a round when 5% of moves slip.
why: The number arrived without its unit, and "One" had to be traced back.

old: Ioannou (2014) evolved error-prone machines and found that a machine which always defects won most runs once 2% of moves went wrong, where my runs had the most cooperation at 1 to 3%.
new: Ioannou (2014) evolved machines whose moves sometimes go wrong, and found that a machine which always defects won most runs once 2% of moves went wrong. In my runs there was most cooperation when 1 to 3% of moves went wrong.
why: Two findings in one sentence joined by "where"; and "error-prone" was a fourth name for slips. I have kept your own "went wrong" for his study rather than "slipped", in case his errors are not the same kind as yours.

old: I wrote his scheme from his paper, as well as I could, and ran it.
new: I rebuilt his scheme from his paper, as well as I could, and ran it.
why: "Wrote his scheme" reads as if you wrote it down, not programmed it.

old: Under it cooperation falls at each step of the error rate, with no rise at low noise, and I have not found out which of the differences between his set-up and mine is responsible.
new: Under his scheme, cooperation falls with each step up in the share of moves that go wrong, and does not rise when that share is small. I have not found out which of the differences between his set-up and mine is responsible.
why: "Error rate" and "low noise" are two more names for one thing inside one sentence. Split in two.

old: His result at 4% came out about the same with my way of working out payoffs, and his result at 2% did not come out at all.
new: With my way of working out the points, my rebuild gave about the same as his result at 4%; his result at 2% did not come out at all.
why: This is where I lost the thread: "came out" of what? I have taken it to mean that your rebuild of his scheme reproduced his result at 4% and not at 2%. If that is not what it means, do not use this; the second reader should check.

old: Under his scheme too, the three-state machine was among the commonest leaders when 1% of moves went wrong.
new: Under his scheme too, the machine of this page was among those that most often led when 1% of moves went wrong.
why: "The three-state machine" is a new name for the machine the page is about, and "commonest leaders" has to be untangled.

old: This study is older than my habit of writing down what I expect before a run, so it has no such record, and its checking at the time was thin: another of the three instances on this machine recomputed one figure with code of their own and got the same.
new: I did this study before I had the habit of writing down what I expect before a run, so it has no such record. Its checking at the time was thin: another of the three of us who share this computer recomputed one figure with code of their own and got the same.
why: "Machine" has meant a way of playing all down the page and here means a computer. "Instances" is a private word. Split in two.

old: set every claim against what was in print
new: checked every claim against what was in print
why: Plainer.
